Keeps apart from a9e01: there one round, here the map of roles and loops. Timeline: the matching tool bought in 2021; in May 2024 (after Latent.Space's post of 30 June 2023 named the title) the maker added 'AI Engineer' and 'Applied AI Engineer', both pointing to its 2021 machine-learning list of 9 skills, because it counted AI as a kind of machine learning; the firm's 14 AI placements since 2021 were all 'ML Engineer' training jobs, which fitted that list. Thursday 10 December 2026: the client posts 'Applied AI Engineer'. Tuesday 15 December, 17:30: the client emails that the same job is also posted as 'Forward-Deployed Engineer' to widen the net; 21:00: 20 CVs run against both adverts, 40 pairs; 23:40: she prints both shortlists onto one page for the call and sees the same name top of one and bottom of the other. The thread runs to about 00:20; every reply's Part 2 starts at 00:30 (reading by hand: 00:30 to 08:00 is 450 minutes, 22 of 40 pairs). Wednesday 16 December, 08:00: the client call. Given data, all in the sim: hers is CV 14, 1 of 9 skills (Python), 11 of 12 duties, 3 years; every other CV shows 2 to 9 of 9 and 2 to 10 of 12; 17 of the other 19 have more than 3 years; the 14 placements and the keep-at-least-7 rule for retraining; the five rounds both adverts name; 20 minutes a pair by hand. Option 0's Part 2: Wednesday 13 January 2027. Cold case: 3 months later, events from 16 December 2026 to Monday 8 March 2027. Personal data in CVs stated conditionally, not legal advice; the candidate and client are unnamed; no real employer or advert is named or quoted. Sources read 16 October 2026; the interview-loop figures come from a secondary source and are labelled so.
title: The Crossroads

post.author: u/top_and_bottom_emerentia
post.title: I'm a recruiter. Tonight our matching tool put one candidate at the top of one shortlist and the bottom of the other. The client says both adverts are the same job.

blocks.text: I'm a recruiter at a small firm that places people in tech jobs. A client tells us about a job; we find candidates and send the best few, a list called a shortlist. In the evenings I study AI (artificial intelligence) engineering myself.
Every candidate sends a CV, short for curriculum vitae: a page or two about their work. Our matching tool, bought in 2021, scores each CV against a job advert in three steps.

First, it reads the advert's title and looks it up in its title list. Second, a known title points to a list of skills; an unknown title falls back to the advert's duties, the work the job says it does. Last, it counts how many of those the CV shows: found out of listed, as a score out of 100, rounded. Then it ranks the CVs, and I send the client the top five.

In May 2024 the tool's maker added two titles, 'AI Engineer' and 'Applied AI Engineer'. It counted AI as a kind of machine learning, ML for short: teaching a program from piles of data, which is called training. So both titles point to its 2021 ML list of 9 skills.
That never mattered to us. Our 14 AI placements since 2021, the jobs we filled, were all titled 'ML Engineer', and they really were training jobs. The list fitted.

Tonight's client wants one engineer to build AI systems inside its customers' businesses, working at the customer's side. That kind of engineer is called forward-deployed. On Thursday 10 December it posted the job as 'Applied AI Engineer'. At 17:30 today, Tuesday 15 December, it emailed: same job, also posted as 'Forward-Deployed Engineer', to widen the net. Our tool doesn't know that title.

Both adverts list the same 12 duties and the same interview rounds: the stages a candidate passes, one after another, before an offer. The whole set is called a loop. Here it is, copied from the adverts:

blocks.title: INTERVIEW ROUNDS, BOTH ADVERTS
items: 1. A screening call with the client's recruiter
3. AI system design: designing a whole AI product out loud
4. A take-home: a task done at home and handed in
5. A customer conversation: a role-play with a pretend client
blocks.sig: The same five under both titles.

blocks.text: I had 20 CVs. At 21:00 I ran all 20 against both adverts, 40 pairs, then wrote up another client's list. Our call is at 08:00 tomorrow.
At 23:40 I printed both shortlists onto one page for the call. The same name sat at the top of one and at the bottom of the other.
Each line below: the advert, what the tool scored her against, how many it found, the score, and her place of 20.

Forward-Deployed Engineer  12 duties (title unknown)  11 of 12  92  1st of 20
Applied AI Engineer        2021 ML list, 9 skills     1 of 9    11  20th of 20
She builds assistants that answer questions on top of models, programs someone else already trained, and has run workshops for clients. She also writes evals, tests with known right answers.
Of the 9 skills her CV shows one: Python, a programming language. Of the 12 duties it shows 11.

Left: Applied AI Engineer is on the title list and points to the 2021 ML list of 9 skills; her CV shows 1 of 9, Python only, a score of 11, 20th of 20. Right: Forward-Deployed Engineer is not on the title list, so the tool falls back to the advert's 12 duties; her CV shows 11 of 12, a score of 92, 1st of 20.

notes.text: Tuesday 15 December: run at 21:00, printed at 23:40
One CV, one job, two titles: 1 of 9 is 11; 11 of 12 is 92 (rounded)

blocks.caption: Drawn at 23:45 from the two shortlists. The same CV, the same 12 duties, the same five rounds. Under 'Applied AI Engineer' the tool scored her against the 2021 ML list and found 1 of 9, Python: 11, last of 20. Under 'Forward-Deployed Engineer' it didn't know the title, fell back to the advert's duties and found 11 of 12: 92, first of 20. I did the sums by hand: 1 ÷ 9 and 11 ÷ 12. The tool was right both times.

blocks.text: The client says it's one job. In my notebook tonight: what is this job, really? The call is at 08:00. What should I change before then?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that office is haunted, and the tool's sums are right. Titles vary by company: the same work goes by several names, and one name can cover different work. For what it's worth, interview-prep writers report that a typical loop runs 4 or 5 rounds, with only about one classic algorithms round, a timed puzzle solved in code; that's reported, not audited. The round that tests tonight is the loop itself: which role it is for, and what each round checks. Two questions. What do the 12 duties ask for, and which of them does her CV show? And what kind of jobs was the 2021 list built from?

replies.author: u/top_and_bottom_emerentia
replies.text: Eleven of the 12 are building AI on models that already exist, much of it with the client: meetings, workshops, presenting results. The twelfth is training a model further. Her CV shows the eleven. The 2021 list was built from training jobs: building models from scratch, statistics, that kind of thing.

comments.author: u/placed_since_2021_wilgefort
comments.text: The tool has placed people since 2021; one odd candidate does not make it wrong. If it's behind the times, retrain it: the tool has a button that rebuilds each title's skills list from the CVs of the people your firm actually placed. Let it learn from real hires, not from one night's hunch.

replies.author: u/top_and_bottom_emerentia
replies.text: Our AI placements since 2021: 14, all titled 'ML Engineer'.

replies.author: u/placed_since_2021_wilgefort
replies.text: Then 14 real hires. That's evidence. Tonight is one CV.

comments.author: u/ten_years_beats_three_cunegund
comments.text: Skills lists go stale; years don't. Rank by years of experience and the title stops mattering: whoever has done the work longest goes first.

replies.author: u/top_and_bottom_emerentia
replies.text: She has 3 years. Seventeen of the other 19 have more, most of it spent training models.

comments.author: u/read_them_all_gudula
comments.text: Stop trusting the tool tonight. Read every advert and CV yourself. You know what the job is better than a 2021 list does.

replies.author: u/top_and_bottom_emerentia
replies.text: I've timed it: about 20 minutes a pair, and there are 40 pairs. And CVs hold personal data, details about a real person. Where a data protection rule, or a rule on automated decisions in hiring, applies, how a tool scores them matters as well as the score. Not legal advice.

reply.prompt: The client call is at 08:00 on Wednesday 16 December. What should I change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add Applied AI Engineer to the title list as forward-deployed work.
options.verdict: One title fixed, the rule kept
options.part2: At 00:30 I added 'Applied AI Engineer' to the title list as another name for forward-deployed work. The tool doesn't know forward-deployed work, so that advert fell back to its duties too: 11 of 12 (92), 1st of 20, the same as the other title. The call at 08:00 went smoothly. On Wednesday 13 January the client's second team posted the same job as 'AI Engineer', the other title the maker had pointed at the 2021 list. The same CV scored 1 of 9 (11) again, 20th of 20, and I only found out because she rang to ask why we hadn't put her forward.
options.senior: An alias fixes the one title you noticed. The fault is the rule underneath: a title points to a skills list, and the list was written for 2021's training jobs. 'AI Engineer' still points there, so the next advert with that title scores the same CV 1 of 9 (11). Titles vary by company and change every year; a list keyed on them needs a new entry for each, and only gets one after someone has been ranked wrongly.

options.text: Retrain the matching tool on the firm's past AI placements since 2021.
options.part2: At 00:30 I pressed retrain. It read our 14 placements since 2021, all 'ML Engineer', and rebuilt each title's list from the skills at least 7 of the 14 CVs showed: training models from scratch, PyTorch, statistics and the rest. The same 9 skills. Nothing else came close: evals showed up in 3 of the 14 CVs, client workshops in 1. 'Applied AI Engineer' still scored her 1 of 9 (11), 20th of 20. At 08:00 the client asked why its one job had two shortlists that disagreed about the same person, and I had no answer.
options.senior: Retraining teaches the tool what your past jobs looked like. The firm's past AI jobs were training jobs, so it learned the training list again: the same 9 skills. A tool trained on yesterday's placements can only score today's work as yesterday's. And the data that would fix it, people placed in forward-deployed jobs, can't build up while the tool ranks them last.

options.text: Read every AI advert and CV by hand tonight before the 08:00 call.
options.verdict: Right every time, and too slow
options.part2: From 00:30 I read pair by pair, about 20 minutes each, starting with her two. Both were plain: 11 of the 12 duties, under either title. By 08:00 I had read 22 of the 40 pairs. The other 18 went to the call unread, and I hadn't slept. Every pair I read, I read right. But the night needed 800 minutes, 13 h 20 min, and it had 450 left in it; and tomorrow the tool would score the next adverts the same way.
options.senior: Reading by hand is the honest check: a person who knows the work reads the duties, not the title, and gets it right. But 40 pairs at 20 minutes is 800 minutes, 13 h 20 min, against 7 h 30 min left before the call, and it fixes nothing for tomorrow. Keep it as a check on a sample of the tool's work, not as a nightly replacement for it.

options.text: Score each CV on the advert's duties and rounds, never on its title.
options.part2: At 00:30 I turned the title list off for AI adverts, so both fell back to their 12 duties, and added each advert's five rounds beside them. Then I sorted both jobs by role family: roles grouped by the work and the interview loop, not the title. Building on existing models, at a client's side, with a customer conversation in the loop: forward-deployed or applied. Both adverts landed there, and she scored 11 of 12 (92), 1st of 20, under both titles. At 08:00 the client agreed: one job, one shortlist. I told her which rounds the loop holds and what each tests, the customer conversation above all. Whether she gets the job is the client's decision; I can't promise it.
options.senior: Score the work, not the name. The duties say what the job does and the rounds say how it's tested; together they place a job in one of five role families: AI engineer, forward-deployed or applied, ML, research, inference. Both adverts sit in the same family, so both score her 11 of 12 (92). A list keyed on 2021 titles scores today's work as yesterday's. The cost: someone has to keep the family map current, and read any advert whose duties and rounds disagree.

sim.title: Score one CV against one job under two titles
sim.lede: You're the recruiter at 21:00 on Tuesday 15 December 2026, both adverts just run. No real model runs here: every count is given data. 20 CVs, numbered 1 to 20; hers is CV 14. Her CV shows 1 of the 2021 ML list's 9 skills (training models from scratch, PyTorch, statistics, feature engineering, experiment tracking, data pipelines, training on GPUs, reading research papers, Python: she shows Python only), 11 of the advert's 12 duties, and 3 years of experience. Every other CV shows 2 to 9 of the 9 skills and 2 to 10 of the 12 duties; 17 of them have more than 3 years. The 12 duties, the same in both adverts: 7 building on existing models, 4 with the client, 1 fine-tuning a model on the client's examples (the one she doesn't show). Both adverts name the same rounds: a screening call, coding, AI system design, a take-home, a customer conversation. The title list: 'AI Engineer' and 'Applied AI Engineer' point to the 9 skills; 'Forward-Deployed Engineer' is unknown and falls back to the duties. Retraining rebuilds the list from the skills at least 7 of the firm's 14 placements since 2021 show (all 'ML Engineer'). Reading by hand takes about 20 minutes a pair; the replies start at 00:30, after the thread, and 00:30 to 08:00 is 450 minutes. Scores are found out of listed, as a share of 100, rounded.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening state is 'applied ai engineer' on the title list: 1 of 9 (11), 20th of 20. Switch the advert to 'forward-deployed engineer': 11 of 12 (92), 1st of 20. Add the alias and try 'ai engineer'. Turn on retrained and read the list it rebuilds. Switch the basis to duties and rounds, by role family, and read both adverts. Rank by years. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the office was haunted, and the tool's sums were right. It scored by title. 'Applied AI Engineer' points to a 2021 machine-learning list of 9 skills, and her CV shows 1 of 9 (11). 'Forward-Deployed Engineer' isn't on the list, so the tool fell back to the advert's 12 duties, and her CV shows 11 of 12 (92). One job, two titles, two lists: a list keyed on 2021 titles scores today's work as yesterday's.

steps.title: How the tool scores, step by step.
steps.text: First, it reads the advert's title. Second, it looks the title up in its title list: a known title points to a skills list, and an unknown one falls back to the duties written in the advert. Third, it counts how many items on that list the CV shows. Last, it turns that into found out of listed, as a share of 100, rounded, and ranks the CVs. What can go wrong: the first two steps decide what is counted before the CV is read at all. 'Applied AI Engineer' pointed to the 2021 list, so her CV was counted against 9 training skills and found 1, Python: 1 of 9 (11). 'Forward-Deployed Engineer' was unknown, so the duties were counted: 11 of 12 (92). The counting was right both times; the list was chosen by the name.

steps.title: Why it never showed before.
steps.text: The maker added 'AI Engineer' and 'Applied AI Engineer' in May 2024, and pointed both at its 2021 machine-learning list, because it counted AI as a kind of machine learning. The firm's 14 AI placements since 2021 were all titled 'ML Engineer', and they really were training jobs, so the list fitted them. What can go wrong: nobody had scored one CV against two titles for the same job. On Tuesday 15 December the client posted its job a second time under a new title, to widen the net, and the two shortlists put the same person first and last.

steps.title: Five role families, told apart by the work and the loop.
steps.text: Group roles by the work they do and the interview they use, and you get five families. An AI engineer builds products on models that already exist: lookup over documents, agents, evals; the loop usually holds coding, AI system design and a take-home. A forward-deployed or applied AI engineer does the same work at a client's side, and the loop adds a customer conversation. An ML engineer trains models from data; the loop leans on ML basics and ML system design. A research engineer or researcher invents new methods; expect talks through research papers, and often a PhD. An inference engineer makes models answer fast and cheaply; expect GPUs, the chips models run on, a systems language and performance work. What can go wrong: titles vary by company, so the same family hides under many names, and one name can cover two families.

steps.title: The loop, round by round.
steps.text: A loop is the set of interview rounds a candidate passes, in order. Interview-prep writers report that a typical one runs 4 or 5 rounds, with only about one classic algorithms round; that comes from secondary sources, not audited counts. This client's runs: first, a screening call, testing whether you can explain your work; second, a coding test; third, AI system design, testing whether you ask about requirements, data, model, evals, safety and cost in that order (a9e01); fourth, a take-home, testing whether you build, measure and write it up honestly (a9e02); last, a customer conversation, testing whether you can explain a trade-off to a client and handle pushback (a9e03, a9e04). What can go wrong: a candidate prepares for the title, not the loop, and walks into a round they never practised.

steps.title: The course on one map.
steps.text: LATENT has walked the map in order. Season 1, how models talk; 2, building with them; 3, giving them knowledge by lookup; 4, agents; 5, evals; 6, running them in production; 7, security; 8, adapting models by fine-tuning; 9, the job itself. Seasons 1 to 9 are the AI engineer's and the forward-deployed engineer's ground. Season 8 is where the ML engineer's training work begins to overlap. Season 10 goes to the inference engineer's ground: making models fast and cheap to serve. What can go wrong: reading the map by title again. Each family is defined by its work and its loop, so check both in every advert.

diagram.aria: The whole LATENT course on one map. Top row, seasons 1 to 5: how it talks, building, knowledge, agents, evals. Middle row, seasons 6 to 10: production, security, adapting, the job, inference. Bottom row, the five role families: AI engineer, the ground of seasons 1 to 9; research, new methods, papers and often a PhD; ML engineer, under season 8, trains models; forward-deployed, under season 9, adds a customer round; inference, under season 10, serves models fast. A note says titles vary by company, and the work and the loop place a job.

notes.text: LATENT on one map: ten seasons, five role families
Titles vary by company; the work and the loop place a job

explain.caption: Read the top two rows in order: the ten seasons of LATENT, from how a model talks to the job itself, and then Season 10, inference. The bottom row is the five role families. The AI engineer's ground is Seasons 1 to 9; Season 8 is where the ML engineer's training work overlaps; Season 9 adds the forward-deployed engineer's client rounds; Season 10 is the inference engineer's. Research sits beyond this course: new methods, papers, often a PhD.

fix.title: The fix: score the duties and the rounds, by role family, never the title
fix.text: Turn the title list off for AI adverts, so every advert is scored on its own duties. Read the rounds each advert names beside them. Place each job in one of five role families by its work and its loop: AI engineer, forward-deployed or applied, ML, research, inference. Both of tonight's adverts are forward-deployed or applied, and both score her 11 of 12 (92), 1st of 20. Then tell each shortlisted candidate which rounds the loop holds and what each tests. Keep a reading by hand for a sample each week, to check the tool's work, and for any advert whose duties and rounds point to different families.

limits: Duties are written by people. An advert that copies an old ML advert's duties will score candidates as ML, whatever the job is; reading the rounds beside the duties catches some of this, not all.

The five families are a map for 2026, and the lines between them move: the Latent.Space post itself calls the API line permeable. Someone has to keep the map current, or it becomes the next 2021 list.

A score is a count of what a CV shows, not a judgment of the person, and it says nothing about whether a candidate will be hired. Where a rule on automated decisions in hiring applies, a person should review the shortlist. Not legal advice.

explain.seniorTake: A title is a label someone chose; the duties and the rounds are the job. Score a CV against what the job does, and read the loop to see how it will be tested; together they place a job in one of five role families, and they don't change when a client renames the advert. A list keyed on 2021 titles scores today's work as yesterday's. The same goes for your own career: read an advert's duties and its interview rounds before its title, and prepare for the loop, round by round, not for the name. The round that tests this is the loop itself: expect 'what is the difference between an AI engineer and an ML engineer, and how are they interviewed?'

realWorld.title: Latent.Space: titles are flawed
realWorld.text: Latent.Space's post The Rise of the AI Engineer (30 June 2023) says: All job titles are flawed, but some are useful. The tool treated a title as the job; the post treats it as a rough label.

realWorld.title: Latent.Space: the API line
realWorld.text: The same post draws a line at the API, short for application programming interface: the doorway a program uses to ask a model provider for an answer. It says: There will be much more capacity for AI Engineers on the other side of the API line to use models, rather than train them. Her CV sits on that side; the 2021 list sits on the training side.

realWorld.title: Interview loops: four or five rounds
realWorld.text: An interview-prep article of 23 July 2026, a secondary source, says a typical 2026 loop for an applied-AI or LLM engineer role runs four or five rounds, and only one of them looks like a classic algorithms interview. Tonight's adverts name five rounds, one of them a coding test.

realWorld.title: Interview loops: the customer round
realWorld.text: The same article says: The customer-conversation round is the one candidates underestimate. On the AI engineer's side of the work it also says: You don’t train the model. Both fit the client's loop, and neither fits the 2021 list.

realWorld.title: Chip Huyen, AI Engineering (O'Reilly, 2025)
realWorld.text: The author's books page describes it in one sentence: This book discusses AI engineering: the process of building applications with readily available foundation models. A foundation model is a large model trained once and used by many builders. Named here as the book on the AI engineer's work; no chapter is cited.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.34: privacy and protection of PII
realWorld.text: A third-party guide titles the control Privacy and Protection of PII and says it covers the storage, privacy and protection of Personal Identifiable Information (PII) in all its forms. A CV is such information; check the wording in your own copy of the standard.

asked: What is the difference between an AI engineer and an ML engineer, and how are they interviewed?
Here is an advert. Which role is this loop for, and what does each round test?
interview.answer: I'd tell them apart by the work and the loop, not the title, because titles vary by company. An AI engineer builds products on models that already exist: lookup over documents, agents, evals, and the safety and cost around them. Their loop usually holds a coding round, an AI system design round and a take-home that builds and measures something. An ML engineer trains models from data, so their loop leans on ML basics, statistics and ML system design. A forward-deployed or applied AI engineer does the AI engineer's work at a client's side, and the loop adds a customer conversation. Research roles invent new methods and talk through papers, often with a PhD; inference roles make models fast and cheap, with GPUs and a systems language. Interview-prep writers report 4 or 5 rounds, with about one classic algorithms round; I'd treat that as reported, not counted. For any advert, I read the duties and the rounds it names, place it in a family, and prepare round by round. The round that tests this is the loop itself.

Details about a real, identifiable person, such as a name and work history on a CV.
A decision about a person made by a program without a person reviewing it, such as dropping a CV from a shortlist by score.
Short for application programming interface: the doorway a program uses to ask another program, such as a model provider, for an answer.
A large model trained once on broad data and used by many builders, who build on it instead of training their own.
Short for graphics processing unit: the chip models train and run on. Inference engineers work close to it.
A programming language for fast, low-level code, such as C++ or Rust. Inference loops often test one.
Short for Doctor of Philosophy: the highest university research degree. Often asked for in research roles.
A newsletter and podcast about AI engineering. Its 2023 post The Rise of the AI Engineer named the role.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A control 5.34 covers privacy and protection of PII.
Short for personally identifiable information: personal data that can point to one person, such as a CV.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012. Among its obligations: consent, and purpose limitation (use personal data only for purposes a person would expect).
Singapore's Data Protection Trustmark: a certification that an organisation handles personal data in line with the PDPA.

atWork: Look for a tool that scores people or work by a label someone chose: a title, a team name, a category. It is a common pattern: the label was mapped to a list years ago, the list fitted the jobs of the time, and nobody notices until the same work arrives under two labels and gets two answers. Ask three things. What does the score count, and who chose that list, and when? Would the same CV score the same under every title the job could carry? And when did a person last read a sample by hand to check? For your own career, do the same: read an advert's duties and its interview rounds before its title, place it in a role family, and prepare round by round. Build Night: this case feeds no Build Night milestone; the season finale, a full forward-deployed engineer simulation, opens with this case's question: which role is this loop for? Standards-readiness note, as these apply to you and not legal advice: CVs hold personal data, so where ISO/IEC 27001:2022 applies, control A.5.34 (privacy and protection of PII) is likely to cover how a matching tool stores and uses them; and for Singapore's DPTM, the PDPA's purpose limitation and consent obligations are likely to apply where a tool scores CVs, so candidates should know their CV will be scored, and for what. Where a rule on automated decisions in hiring applies, a person should review any shortlist a tool ranks. Building this in now costs far less than rebuilding the scoring, or the consent, at audit time.

recall.prompt: A friend is preparing for two interviews. Advert A is titled 'ML Engineer', but its duties are building a support assistant on a model rented from a provider, and its rounds include a take-home. Advert B is titled 'AI Engineer', but its duties are training new models from the company's own data. What should she prepare for each?

keyIdeas.idea: Go by the duties and the rounds, not the title
A is AI engineer work: prepare AI system design and evals, building on existing models
B is ML engineer work: prepare ML basics, statistics and ML system design

recall.model: Go by the duties and the rounds, not the title: titles vary by company. Advert A builds on an existing model, so it's AI engineer work whatever it's called: she should prepare AI system design, evals and a take-home that builds and measures something. Advert B trains models from data, so it's ML engineer work: prepare ML basics, statistics and ML system design. Then she should ask each recruiter for the full loop and prepare round by round.

recall.prompt: The tool scores her CV against the 2021 list of 9 skills and finds 1. Against the advert's 12 duties it finds 11. What do the two scores read, rounded?
recall.why: A score is found out of listed, as a share of 100: 1 of 9 is 11.1, read as 11; 11 of 12 is 91.7, read as 92. The same CV, the same job, two lists chosen by two titles.

recall.prompt: An interviewer asks: what is the difference between an AI engineer and an ML engineer, and how is each interviewed?

keyIdeas.idea: An AI engineer builds products on models that already exist
An ML engineer trains models from data
The loops differ: AI system design and a take-home for one, ML basics and ML system design for the other

recall.model: An AI engineer builds products on models that already exist: lookup over documents, agents, evals, and the safety and cost around them. An ML engineer trains models from data. Their loops differ: the AI engineer usually faces coding, AI system design and a take-home that builds and measures something; the ML engineer faces ML basics, statistics and ML system design. Titles vary by company, so I'd read the duties and the rounds to tell which one an advert really is.

recall.prompt: 40 pairs of advert and CV, about 20 minutes each, read from 00:30 until an 08:00 call. How many pairs can be read?
recall.why: 00:30 to 08:00 is 7 h 30 min, 450 minutes; 450 ÷ 20 = 22 whole pairs, with 10 minutes over. All 40 would need 800 minutes, 13 h 20 min. Reading by hand is right every time, and too slow to replace the tool.

recall.prompt: Which round does a forward-deployed or applied AI engineer's loop usually add to an AI engineer's?
options: A customer conversation with a pretend client
recall.why: Forward-deployed engineers do the AI engineer's work at a client's side, so the loop adds a customer conversation: explaining a trade-off and handling pushback. Paper discussions belong to research roles, GPU performance to inference roles.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Since 16 December the firm scores every AI advert on its duties and the rounds it names, sorted into five role families, and the client's one job has had one shortlist. On Monday 8 March a new client posted an advert titled 'AI Engineer'. Its duties: make the client's own models answer faster and cheaper on its own GPUs, the chips the models run on. Its rounds: coding, a systems language (C++ or Rust), and GPU performance. My colleague wants to send our best candidates for building assistants, because the title says AI Engineer.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Which role is this, and who belongs on the shortlist?

keyIdeas.idea: The duties and rounds place it in the inference family, not the AI engineer family
Shortlist people with performance and low-level experience, and tell them the rounds to prepare

coldCase.model: It's an inference role: the duties are serving the client's own models with less delay and at lower cost, and the rounds test exactly that. Ignore the title; titles vary by company, and this one would put assistant builders in front of a job they haven't trained for. Shortlist people with performance work on models, low-level code and hardware behind them, score their CVs on these duties, and tell each one the rounds to prepare for: coding, the systems language, and the performance round. That's Season 10's ground.
